misconceptions.citation: Early rational-number concept development literature on the part-whole construct (Behr, Post & Lesh).
misconceptions.cognitive_origin: Whole-number-count bias: before a part-whole scheme develops, children read '3/4' as two independent counts read top-to-bottom ('a three and a four') rather than a single quantity describing parts out of a whole.
sprout_forbidden: stating the fraction names one quantity before resolution
misconceptions.title: A fraction is two separate whole numbers, not one quantity

misconceptions.citation: Research on children's partitioning strategies and the equal-parts requirement in early fraction instruction.
misconceptions.cognitive_origin: Children over-attend to the COUNT of pieces and under-attend to their SIZE, so any shape divided into N regions is labeled '1/N' regardless of whether the regions are equal — a failure to encode equal partitioning as a defining feature of a fraction.
misconceptions.title: Unequal partitions still count as a valid fraction

misconceptions.citation: Whole-number bias literature; Siegler et al. on fraction magnitude.
misconceptions.cognitive_origin: Whole-number bias — the child transfers whole-number ordering to the denominator, since 8 > 4.
misconceptions.title: Larger denominator means larger fraction

misconceptions.citation: Literature on componential vs. proportional reasoning in fraction equivalence.
misconceptions.cognitive_origin: Children treat numerator and denominator as independent whole-number counts, so scaling both by the same factor looks like making a different, bigger fraction rather than preserving the same part-whole ratio — a failure to see multiplicative equivalence.
misconceptions.title: Scaling numerator and denominator together changes a fraction's value

misconceptions.citation: Fraction-comparison strategy literature on componential (part-by-part) reasoning.
misconceptions.cognitive_origin: An overgeneralization of the (correct, unit-fraction-only) rule 'more pieces means a smaller piece' to fractions whose numerators also differ: the child compares only denominators and ignores the numerator entirely (e.g., judging 3/8 < 1/4 because 8 > 4).
misconceptions.title: Bigger denominator always means a smaller fraction, even across different numerators

misconceptions.citation: Literature on the part-whole-only conception of fractions and the transition to fractions greater than one.
misconceptions.cognitive_origin: Early fraction experience is almost entirely parts of a single whole (pizza slices, pie charts), so 'fraction' gets encoded as inherently less than one; a numerator larger than the denominator is treated as an error rather than a quantity greater than one whole.
sprout_forbidden: stating a fraction can be greater than one whole before resolution
misconceptions.title: A fraction can never be greater than one whole

misconceptions.citation: Research on children's difficulty transferring fraction understanding from area models to set/group models.
misconceptions.cognitive_origin: When asked for a fraction of a GROUP of objects rather than a single shape, children map the wrong number in the fraction onto the partitioning step, using the numerator as the divisor instead of the denominator — a failure to transfer the part-whole model from area to a set/group model.
sprout_forbidden: stating you divide by the denominator before resolution
misconceptions.title: Fraction of a set means dividing by the numerator, not the denominator

misconceptions.citation: The 'add straight across' bug is among the most widely documented fraction-arithmetic errors in mathematics-education research.
misconceptions.cognitive_origin: The 'add straight across' bug: children apply whole-number addition procedures directly to both parts of the fraction (1/4 + 1/4 -> 2/8) because they have not yet encoded that the denominator names the unit size, which stays fixed when the pieces being combined are already the same size.
misconceptions.title: Adding fractions means adding numerators and denominators separately
